name: Smart casual

lead: Smart casual is a Western dress code that sits between casual wear and a lounge suit. It lets people look neat and deliberate in settings that do not call for formal dress.

It helps looks through clothing: well-fitting, clean pieces such as a blazer, chinos, a collared shirt or dress shoes create a more polished impression. Surveys of how doctors' attire affects patient impressions show clothing choice shapes first impressions in professional settings.

paras: Men commonly combine a dress shirt or polo, chinos or trousers and leather shoes, sometimes with an odd-coloured blazer; ties and jeans depend on the setting. Women's examples include dresses, pantsuits and neat, muted outfits with accessories. Fit, cleanliness and pressed fabrics are recurring themes.
No health risks. The main difficulty is ambiguity: the term has no fixed rules, and interpretation differs between venues and countries.

angle.text: Smart casual gives a ready outfit formula that makes someone look put-together in everyday and semi-formal settings. The look comes directly from the clothes and fit.

lead: Smart casual is an ambiguously defined Western dress code between casual clothing and a proper lounge suit, borrowing some polish from informal formal wear.[1]

It helps people look better by providing a reliable formula for looking neat without formality: tailored or fitted separates, clean fabrics and sensible shoes. Typical men's items include dress shirts, chinos or trousers, polos, dress shoes and blazers, with jeans sometimes accepted depending on the setting.[1]

Studies of clothing in clinical settings, mostly surveys of patient preferences about doctors' attire, find that dress affects first impressions and perceived professionalism, and smart-casual attire is among the styles compared.[2][3][4]
infobox: Dress shirt or polo, chinos, blazer, dress shoes

paras: Smart casual was originally used to describe a lounge suit in an unusual colour and lighter, more casual fabric, sometimes with a more relaxed cut. Once the solid-colour lounge suit became the standard for informal wear, mismatched colours became associated with smart casual.[1]

For women, sources cited by reference works give examples such as dresses, pantsuits and neat, wrinkle-free outfits in muted colours with black or brown heels, plus easy fabrics that are not too dressy.[1]

The term first appeared in print in May 1924 in the Davenport Democrat and Leader in Iowa.[1] By the 1950s it had merged into business casual, and whether a difference between the two exists is disputed.[1] Since the 1960s counterculture, expectations have varied across Western cultures and events, especially for neckties and, in warm climates, jackets.[1]

Several surveys have asked patients how clinicians' clothes affect them. A 2009 survey of 586 patients had them rate photographs of a doctor in scrubs, professional informal and professional formal attire.[4] Other studies looked at surgeons, orthopaedic staff, veterinarians and general physicians, finding that attire influences impressions and confidence, and noting that dress in surgery has moved from suit and tie to smart-casual forms.[5][2][3][6]
Style communities such as Lemmy's malefashionadvice post outfits described as smart casual, for example a mid-blue V-neck sweater look.[7]
No studies found on smart casual as an intervention. Related research consists of attire-perception surveys in healthcare settings.[5][2][3][4][6]
